heading: Observation over generations
intro: Indigenous knowledge systems have always been built on careful, patient observation of the land, water, sky and seasons, shared and tested over many generations. Science today increasingly works alongside that knowledge. These connections show what that looks like here in Edmonton, across Alberta and across Canada.

connections.title: kihcihkaw askî: "This place here is Sacred"
connections.text: In Edmonton's river valley, at 14141 Fox Drive, is kihcihkaw askî, an Indigenous ceremonial and cultural site. Elders chose the nêhiyawêwin (Cree) name, which they say means "This place here is Sacred." The area has long been used for gathering medicines. Guided by an Elders Council and operated by the Indigenous Knowledge & Wisdom Centre, it is a place for traditional teachings, traditional arts and sciences, and intergenerational, land-based learning. It is a reminder that observing the land closely is a way of learning that has happened in this valley for a very long time.

connections.title: Communities that collect their own data
connections.text: In northeastern Alberta, First Nations, Métis organizations and Métis locals run community-based environmental monitoring. Communities set their own priorities, then collect samples from the air, water and land to learn how ecosystems are changing. Projects bring together Indigenous Knowledge and science, and many train youth to do the fieldwork. When the people who live on the land help decide what to measure and where, the data is more likely to answer the questions that matter there.

sources.title: Environment and Climate Change Canada: Indigenous fund for community-based environmental monitoring

connections.title: Sea ice: numbers and knowledge together
connections.text: Across Inuit Nunangat, SmartICE measures sea ice thickness with sensors on the ice and sensors towed behind snowmobiles along travel trails. In Pond Inlet, a community committee called Sikumiut, meaning "people of the ice," runs the work, with members from young hunters to Elders. The thickness readings are quantitative data. Inuit sea ice knowledge adds what experienced ice travellers observe. Together they help people decide when and where travel is safe. Young Inuit are trained to build and run the equipment.

connections.title: Two-Eyed Seeing
connections.text: Mi'kmaw Elder Albert Marshall of Eskasoni First Nation describes Two-Eyed Seeing, or Etuaptmumk: learning to see with the strengths of Indigenous knowledges through one eye and the strengths of Western science through the other, and using both eyes together. It is one way scientists and communities across Canada approach working with more than one way of knowing.

try: SmartICE combines sensor readings with what experienced ice travellers notice. Which parts are quantitative data and which are qualitative? Why might a community trust the two together more than either one alone?
In community-based monitoring, the community chooses what to measure. How could who asks the question change what data gets collected? Connect your answer to sampling bias.

Observations made the same way, in the same place, over many years are very valuable. Choose one spot near your school. What could you observe there every week this year, and what patterns might you find?

Citation for the lab's existing Lesson 1 note (Knowledge Keepers on Treaty 6 noting when lakes freeze, berries ripen and animals move): I could not find a source that supports that exact sentence, so I propose this sourced rewording, to be applied to the note when you approve this item: "Careful, long-term observation is also part of Indigenous knowledge systems. Métis harvester and writer Conor Kerr, in Treaty 6 territory, describes berries ripening up to two weeks early in some years and moose turning up where they were not expected, and treats these observations as climate knowledge. In some Ininew (Cree) communities in Manitoba, moons are named for what happens on the land, such as the Freezing Up Moon, when ice begins to form." Sources: Conor Kerr, "What the land knows: Métis harvesting narratives as climate knowledge" (Canadian Climate Institute), https://climateinstitute.ca/publications/what-the-land-knows-metis-harvesting-narratives-as-climate-knowledge/ and Wilfred Buck, Opaskwayak Cree Nation, "Thirteen Moons" (Canadian Space Agency), https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/youth-educators/thirteen-moons.asp.
